text.title: Process Mining Tool Shortlist Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules with rationale + source for process-mining-tool-shortlist. Includes terminal skip-this-methodology rule.

rule.statement: Shortlist MUST score each tool against weighted criteria (ingestion fit, query language, visualisation, conformance check, conformance check, total cost of ownership, vendor lock-in); weights agreed with sponsor before scoring.
rule.rationale: Weights chosen after the scores are visible are not weights; they are a justification for a tool someone already favoured, and the exercise then wraps a defensible-looking document around a decision that was never genuinely contested. Omitting them is not neutral either: it weights every criterion equally, so the many easy-to-judge criteria such as visualisation collectively outvote the one that decides the project, which is usually whether the tool can ingest the client's event log at all.

rule.statement: Each tool score MUST cite evidence: vendor demo recording, sample event log result, G2 reference call, hands-on POC; un-anchored scores forbidden.
rule.rationale: Unanchored scores blend hands-on findings with vendor marketing at equal weight, so a datasheet claim about conformance checking becomes indistinguishable from an observed result on the client's own log. The anchor is also what makes the shortlist contestable in a useful way: a sponsor can interrogate a demo recording or a reference call, but a bare score offers nothing to push against, so disagreement collapses into a clash of authority.

rule.statement: Shortlist MUST contain at least 3 tools (commercial + open-source); single-tool shortlists are not shortlists.
rule.rationale: A single option cannot be evaluated, only rationalised, because "good enough" means nothing without something to measure it against. Requiring an open-source entry alongside commercial ones stops the comparison collapsing into three vendors sharing the same pricing model and the same assumptions; it forces a materially different cost and effort profile onto the table, which is frequently what reframes the sponsor's original question.

rule.statement: Each shortlist row MUST have a single named owner who ran the evaluation; consensus authorship is forbidden.
rule.rationale: A consensus score has no author, so its reasoning cannot be recovered: when the tool disappoints three months in, nobody can say what was actually tested and what was assumed. Naming the evaluator per row also exposes uneven depth, which the table otherwise conceals, because a score from a hands-on proof of concept and one from a ten-minute datasheet skim look identical once both are a number in a cell.

rule.statement: Shortlist carries a review-by date (default 6 months); past that, vendor landscape may have shifted enough to invalidate.
rule.rationale: A shortlist gets reused precisely because redoing it is expensive, and nothing on its face tells the next reader how old its findings are. The process-mining market moves through acquisitions, pricing-model changes and feature-parity shifts, so a two-year-old ranking can be confidently wrong while reading as authoritative. The review-by date puts staleness on the document itself instead of relying on the reader to know the vendor history.

rule.statement: Final pick is recorded as an ADR (architecture decision record) attached to the shortlist; tool-pick without ADR is forbidden.
rule.rationale: The shortlist records how the tools compared; it does not record why the winner was chosen, and the two routinely differ because the pick also absorbs constraints the scoring never held, such as a budget cycle or an existing vendor relationship. Without that written down, the next reader sees a tool that failed to top every axis and reopens a decision that was in fact taken correctly, at the price of running the same evaluation twice.

rule.statement: Rejected tools MUST list rejection reason; silent omission is forbidden because the next engagement re-derives the rejection.
rule.rationale: The rejection reason is the most transferable output the exercise produces: it is what stops the next engagement paying full price to rediscover the same blocker. Unexplained absence also reads as oversight rather than as a decision, so a stakeholder or the vendor's account manager can reasonably push the omitted tool back into scope, restarting the evaluation from a position the team already worked through.

rule.statement: If tool choice is already mandated or the scope is below the methodology break-even, return `skipped`.
rule.rationale: Where the tool is already mandated the shortlist cannot change the outcome, and running it anyway produces a document whose main effect is to open an argument the team has no authority to win, at full evaluation cost. Below the break-even scope the spread between candidate tools is smaller than the cost of measuring it, so the exercise consumes more than the decision it informs is worth.
